The thing to remember about Phelps...and just about every other athlete whose sport is, to some degree, specialized with regard to movement...is that his body isn't just fit, it's optimized for the sport in which he competes.

I'm a cyclist myself...and at the peak of my cycling fitness, I was profoundly well-built for it. Big legs, strong lats, a resting heart rate in the 40s. But if you asked me to curl a lot of weight, I couldn't. I was incredibly fit for a sport that required a lot of some parts of my body and not so much of other parts. Cyclists spend thousands of dollars to reduce the weight of their bike by five pounds...it doesn't make any sense at all to carry 10 extra pounds on your body if it does you no good.

Case in point: there was an Olympic skater named Eric Heiden, who won an unprecedented 5 gold medals, setting 4 Olympic records and one world record. He was crazy fit, and his body was actually pretty balanced. He then went into professional cycling, but when it got into mountain stages or hot days, the poor man just died. He had too much body mass (as muscle) in places where it only weighed him down instead of helping him keep up on the bike. He had the legs, he had the cardio...he just had too much else that he had to carry around as well. He was disciplined, he was motivated, and he definitely tried...but the extra weight absolutely killed him. You should have seen the pictures of him in the middle of a peloton during a moderate climb - cyclists around him just having their jerseys half-zipped, getting on with the program, while he was in the center drenched in sweat (it's hard to keep that wet with a 25 mph wind blowing over you), his jersey zipped all the way down, and a look of absolute misery on his face.

So when thinking about how "strong" someone is...keep in mind that you can be the strongest in the world at something, while simultaneously not being all that strong at all with regard to something else. And that will also reflect itself in your body weight. A competitive athlete in a sport like cycling, running, or swimming definitely will have a lower BMI than a weightlifter, even though they may have the same percentage of body fat.

BMI is a useful construct, as I see it, and while it's not going to be correct for outliers like bodybuilders or weightlifters who have bulked up on muscle, in those cases it's profoundly obvious that these people are not out of shape. If someone has a high BMI and claims it's because BMI doesn't work...ask them what sport they do, and what their benchmarks are for it. What's their deadlift/squat/bench personal best? How far have they cycled/run/swam at one time, and how long did it take them? No fatty will have an answer that will work (unless they lie, and then they tend to say things like "I ran a 3-minute mile.")
